title: Boethius in prison
hook: awaiting execution around 524, Boethius writes The Consolation of Philosophy, where Philosophy visits him as a woman (Consolation 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aristotle's middle, the right amount for you, here, now. Your line was the mean. Which habit took a step toward the middle? This week: Epicurus on death and friends, Seneca the scout, the skeptics, Socrates, Aristotle. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

A man who had everything is sitting in a cell. Not long ago he held high office in Italy. His two sons were made consuls on the same day, and he gave the speech. Now he's been accused of treason, condemned without a real hearing, and he's waiting to be killed. He does the natural thing in a dark hour: he writes sad poems about how unfair it all is. And then, in his book, someone walks into the cell. Today: Theodoric.
screen: `FROM HIGH OFFICE TO A CELL.` → `SAD POEMS IN A DARK HOUR.` → `SOMEONE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Boethius was a Roman senator serving Theodoric, the Gothic king who ruled Italy. He was a scholar too, steeped in Greek philosophy. In the book he says he was accused of treason partly for defending another senator, and condemned far away, without being heard. He was executed not long after. Second, the visitor. The Consolation of Philosophy opens with Boethius weeping over verses, the Muses of poetry gathered round him. Then a woman appears: hard to measure, sometimes ordinary height, sometimes her head seems to touch the sky. Her robe is woven with Greek letters and a ladder between them, and it's torn. She's Philosophy. She sends the Muses away, and sits down on his bed. Third, the torn robe. She explains it: after Socrates and Plato, rival crowds tried to seize her, Epicureans and Stoics among them, each tearing away a scrap and thinking they had the whole. It's a fitting image after this week of neighbors. Fourth, what kind of book it is. Boethius was a Christian; he wrote works of theology. Yet the Consolation never names Christ and argues from philosophy alone. Scholars still debate why. What he does is talk with Philosophy, in prose and poetry, about fortune, happiness and God, while waiting to die. And it begins with something anyone can do in a hard hour: stop only lamenting, and let a wiser voice, even your own, ask you some questions.
screen: `A SENATOR CONDEMNED.` · `A WOMAN WALKS IN: PHILOSOPHY.` · `HER ROBE TORN BY RIVAL SCHOOLS.` · `A CHRISTIAN ARGUING FROM REASON.` · then, large: `PHILOSOPHY VISITS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard in your life right now, or recently. Let yourself feel the complaint, the unfairness of it. Now imagine a calm, wise presence sitting down beside you: Philosophy, or a grandparent, or the best version of yourself. What's the first question they'd ask you? Not advice. A question. If you have something to write with, write it down, and begin an answer in a line or two. The bell holds the time.
Theodoric. The Gothic king Boethius served as a Roman senator before being condemned and imprisoned, awaiting execution. Today's word.
Your line: philosophy visits. The next time a complaint starts looping today, invite the wise visitor in, and let her ask one question. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss and injustice, some reading it as a dialogue with their own wiser mind.

fork.setup: you're Boethius, condemned, writing sad verses with the Muses of poetry. Philosophy walks in. what does she do first?

fork.reveal: she drives off the Muses who were feeding his grief, sits beside him, and begins to ask him questions.

original.note: Latin: consolation, comfort. Consolatio Philosophiae, the comfort that philosophy gives.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book of comfort is gentle and sweet.
what it means: a condemned man argues with Philosophy about fortune, happiness and God while waiting to die.

what a scholar hears: the Consolation mixes prose and verse (a Menippean form), its robe carries the letters pi and theta for practical and theoretical philosophy, and it was translated by King Alfred, Chaucer and Elizabeth I.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut unsourced dates ('early 500s', 'around 524') and superlatives ('one of the most powerful officials', 'one of the most read and translated books of the Middle Ages', 'fifteen centuries'); 'what many of us do' no longer speaks for the listener; teach now sticks to what Consolation 1 prose 4 says about the charge; replaced the date match pair and the most-read myth item.
Boethius c. 477–524 (some date the execution to 525); his sons consuls together in 522, when he gave the panegyric; magister officiorum 522; accused while defending Albinus. Confirm.

Philosophy's shifting height, the robe with Π and Θ and a ladder, torn: Consolation 1, prose 1. Epicurean and Stoic mobs tearing her robe: 1, prose 3. She drives away the Muses: 1, prose 1. Sits on his bed: 1, prose 1/2. Confirm.
Boethius's Christianity (the Opuscula Sacra) and the Consolation's silence about Christ: scholarly debate. Confirm hedge.
Translations by Alfred, Chaucer and Elizabeth I: well attested; confirm.
